Wardrobe
word'rōb
n. (the royal or sacred vestry, and the office of its keeper; the post held by Huldah the prophetess's husband)
From Old French warderobe, a place to guard robes. The Hebrew is beged, garment, in a construction meaning keeper of the garments — a real office in the royal and temple establishment.

Biblical Definition

The word occurs twice, in parallel accounts of the same errand, and both times it identifies a man by his job in order to locate his wife. Josiah's men, holding a book of the law found in the temple, are sent to enquire of the LORD: “So Hilkiah the priest, and Ahikam, and Achbor, and Shaphan, and Asahiah, went unto Huldah the prophetess, the wife of Shallum the son of Tikvah, the son of Harhas, keeper of the wardrobe; (now she dwelt in Jerusalem in the college;) and they communed with her” (2 Kings 22:14). Chronicles records it identically (2 Chronicles 34:22). The mission was urgent — “great is the wrath of the LORD that is kindled against us, because our fathers have not hearkened unto the words of this book” (2 Kings 22:13) — and Huldah's answer, delivered in the ordinary form of prophetic speech, both confirmed the coming judgment and granted Josiah a reprieve: “thine eyes shall not see all the evil which I will bring upon this place” (2 Kings 22:20). The keeper of the wardrobe kept the vestments; his wife was consulted by the king's highest officers, in her own house, and the whole reformation of Judah turned on what she said.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines wardrobe as a room or portable closet in which wearing apparel is kept, and also wearing apparel in general.

expand to see more

WARDROBE, n. A room or apartment where clothes are kept.

2. Wearing apparel in general.

VESTRY, n. A room appendant to a church, in which the sacerdotal vestments and sacred utensils are kept.

VESTMENT, n. A garment; some part of clothing or dress; particularly, a long outer garment.

PROPHETESS, n. A female prophet.

Key Scripture

2 Kings 22:14 — "So Hilkiah the priest, and Ahikam, and Achbor, and Shaphan, and Asahiah, went unto Huldah the prophetess, the wife of Shallum the son of Tikvah, the son of Harhas, keeper of the wardrobe; (now she dwelt in Jerusalem in the college;) and they communed with her."

2 Kings 22:13 — "Go ye, enquire of the LORD for me, and for the people, and for all Judah, concerning the words of this book that is found: for great is the wrath of the LORD that is kindled against us, because our fathers have not hearkened unto the words of this book, to do according unto all that which is written concerning us."

2 Kings 22:20 — "Behold therefore, I will gather thee unto thy fathers, and thou shalt be gathered into thy grave in peace; and thine eyes shall not see all the evil which I will bring upon this place. And they brought the king word again."

2 Chronicles 34:22 — "And Hilkiah, and they that the king had appointed, went to Huldah the prophetess, the wife of Shallum the son of Tikvath, the son of Hasrah, keeper of the wardrobe; (now she dwelt in Jerusalem in the college:) and they spake to her to that effect."

Modern Corruption

Huldah is enlisted to overturn the New Testament's ordering of the church, or else quietly passed over by those the ordering protects.

expand to see more

Huldah is regularly produced as proof that Scripture knows no distinction of office between men and women, since the high priest himself came to her for a word from the LORD. The argument moves too fast. Huldah gave a prophetic word in her own house to a delegation; she did not hold the priesthood, did not serve at the altar, and did not exercise rule in the assembly. The New Testament likewise records Philip's four daughters who prophesied and Anna in the temple, alongside the plain instruction that a woman is not to teach nor usurp authority over the man, grounded in the creational order of 1 Timothy 2:13. The offices of elder and deacon are the questions in dispute, and prophetic speech was never restricted the way office is.

The opposite failure belongs to churches that hold the right doctrine and then behave as though women had no part in the life of the covenant people at all. Josiah's reformation — the greatest recorded of any king of Judah — turned on the word of a woman whom the king's officers sought out by name when Jeremiah and Zephaniah were both alive. She is called the prophetess without apology, and her word is recorded as the word of the LORD. Any complementarianism that cannot say that plainly is not the Bible's, and it will keep losing daughters to the framework it refuses to answer.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shomer habbegadim, keeper of the garments — 2 Kings 22:14, 2 Chronicles 34:22; nebiah, prophetess — the title given Huldah, Miriam, Deborah and Anna's counterparts.

expand to see more

Hebrew beged — a garment; in the construction rendered keeper of the wardrobe, Shallum's office.

Hebrew shamar — to keep, to guard; the verb behind the title of the office.

Hebrew nebiah — prophetess; used of Miriam (Exodus 15:20), Deborah (Judges 4:4) and Huldah (2 Kings 22:14).

Hebrew mishneh — the second quarter or district of Jerusalem, rendered the college in the Authorized Version.

2 Kings 22:16-17 records her message: the LORD will bring evil upon this place, according to all the words of the book.

Usage

"“Keeper of the wardrobe” — a real office in the royal establishment."

"“They went unto Huldah the prophetess… and they communed with her” — the king's highest officers, at her house."

"The reformation of Judah turned on what she said."
